sentence_as_it_stands: The safe interval between sessions on any of these agents. [dose figure omitted] is the floor the published series work to, and it rests on those series' schedules rather than on a clearance measurement.
quote: the systemic absorption of corticosteroid was unknown. Finally, the optimum dosage of anesthetics and corticosteroids and the frequency of rejection remain to be determined. … Our study demonstrated that repetitive intracutaneous injections with ropivacaine and methylprednisolone plus standard treatment with acyclovir and tramadol are more effective than the standard treatment alone
corrected_wording: No source measures an interval between sessions for any of these agents. Published schedules vary, from closely spaced sessions (a randomised trial of repeated intracutaneous local anaesthetic–steroid sessions in acute herpes zoster, Cui 2017, PMID 27492741; consecutive-day subcutaneous lidocaine–steroid injections in refractory postherpetic neuralgia, Nguyen 2021, PMID 33855194) to weekly or longer intervals, and each rests on the study's own schedule rather than on a clearance measurement.
notes: Same sentence as claim D072 (other-claim and extra-study entries). The page names no series here, so the stated floor reads as a description of published schedules in general; Cui 2017 spaced its repeated intracutaneous sessions more closely than that floor (schedule in the paper card; not repeated here), and Nguyen 2021 (found by a PubMed search prompted by Cui; not in its reference list) used consecutive-day sessions. Neither measured clearance, so the sentence's main point (no clearance-based interval) stands. Medium rather than high: the correction adds no safety information, because no study measures an inter-session interval either way. Page text read through a masked viewer; its ceilings were not copied.

page: Ropiconest ropivacaína (lower strength, [dose figure omitted] pack) — Farmacia La Paz (Mexico) [Buying Decisions & Info]
section: Why; Why For Purpose; body: Verdict and What would change this
sentence_as_it_stands: Needs More Research: no wheal study of ropivacaine with a pain outcome exists, so its evidence for the purpose is only indirect, from one uncontrolled study of lidocaine wheals. [Why For Purpose: 'No wheal study of ropivacaine with a pain outcome is indexed in PubMed'; What would change this: 'A wheal study of ropivacaine with a pain outcome, in any neuropathic pain condition, would settle the verdict.']
quote: In the current study, we compared the effects of intracutaneous injections with ropivacaine and methylprednisolone in addition to standard treatment of antiviral and oral analgesics with standard treatment in 93 HZ patients for the prevention of PHN. … In the current study, intracutaneous injection using local anesthetics plus corticosteroids resulted in lower pain intensity (VAS) and fewer doses of rescue drug (tramadol) at each follow-up time point
corrected_wording: No study of plain ropivacaine wheals with a pain outcome exists. Ropivacaine mixed with methylprednisolone has been given by repeated intracutaneous injection in a randomised trial in acute herpes zoster, with lower pain scores and less postherpetic neuralgia than standard treatment alone (Cui 2017, PMID 27492741), and by a single intracutaneous injection against saline (Cui 2018, PMID 29153295); neither isolates ropivacaine from the steroid, and neither is in established neuropathic pain or small fibre neuropathy.
notes: Cui 2017 is PubMed-indexed (MeSH 'Injections, Intradermal' and 'Ropivacaine') and is a randomised trial whose intracutaneous injections contained ropivacaine, with pain outcomes, so 'no wheal study of ropivacaine with a pain outcome exists / is indexed in PubMed' is too absolute. The row's Decision ('Needs More Research') and Met Intended Purpose ('Kinda') rest on this absence, and its 'What would change this' names exactly such a study as what would settle the verdict; whether a steroid-confounded trial in acute zoster does so is for the main session to weigh (importance high on that ground, not because the verdict must change). The row's narrower statement that the one anaesthetic-only wheal protocol with an outcome is Mülkoğlu 2020 is not touched. Product strengths and amounts on the row were not copied.

section: PART X — 13. The open gaps, item 1 (and its 'What independent search did find' list)
sentence_as_it_stands: Nobody has measured neuropathic pain relief from an intradermal ropivacaine wheal at any concentration — but the gap is a PARTIAL one and this page previously stated it too absolutely. … Cui 2016 and similar acute-zoster trials use intradermal lidocaine as an active control or co-intervention, always alongside valaciclovir, methylene blue, corticosteroids, methylcobalamin or nerve blocks. None isolates the anaesthetic effect.
quote: In the current study, we compared the effects of intracutaneous injections with ropivacaine and methylprednisolone in addition to standard treatment of antiviral and oral analgesics with standard treatment in 93 HZ patients for the prevention of PHN. … In the current study, intracutaneous injection using local anesthetics plus corticosteroids resulted in lower pain intensity (VAS) and fewer doses of rescue drug (tramadol) at each follow-up time point
corrected_wording: No one has measured neuropathic pain relief from a plain intradermal ropivacaine wheal. Intracutaneous ropivacaine mixed with methylprednisolone has been tested with pain outcomes in randomised trials in acute herpes zoster — repeated injections added to standard treatment (Cui 2017, PMID 27492741) and a single injection against saline (Cui 2018, PMID 29153295) — but the steroid is co-injected, so neither isolates ropivacaine's effect; other acute-zoster trials use intradermal lidocaine alongside antivirals, methylene blue, corticosteroids, methylcobalamin or nerve blocks.
notes: Page tested by another session (S1); recorded as a finding only. The gap is already marked PARTIAL and the bullet's conclusion (none isolates the anaesthetic effect) holds for both Cui trials. What is wrong is the summary's statement that these acute-zoster trials use intradermal lidocaine: for a ropivacaine page, the two randomised trials of intracutaneous ropivacaine (with methylprednisolone) with pain endpoints are the nearest published human clinical data on the drug in skin, and the page does not record them. Gap 2 ('Nobody has used ropivacaine wheals for small fibre neuropathy') stands.

section: 12.3a Protocol design from the closest existing intervention
sentence_as_it_stands: One wheal protocol with a local anaesthetic and a pain outcome has been published: [dose figure omitted] of [dose figure omitted] lidocaine diluted in [dose figure omitted] of saline, [dose figure omitted] wheals [dose figure omitted] apart, [dose figure omitted], with pain lower at 2 and 4 weeks and at 3 months in 20 people with notalgia paresthetica, uncontrolled, and none in small fibre neuropathy (Mülkoğlu 2020, PMID 32416719).
quote: Ninety-three patients with acute thoracic HZ were randomly assigned to receive a standard treatment of antiviral medication with p.o. analgesics or the standard treatment with the addition of repetitive intracutaneous injections of a local anesthetic and steroid mixture.
corrected_wording: One anaesthetic-only wheal protocol with a pain outcome has been published (Mülkoğlu 2020, PMID 32416719: uncontrolled, notalgia paresthetica; none in small fibre neuropathy). A randomised trial of repeated intracutaneous injections of ropivacaine mixed with methylprednisolone, with pain and postherpetic-neuralgia outcomes, has also been published, in acute herpes zoster (Cui 2017, PMID 27492741); its steroid is co-injected, so it does not isolate the anaesthetic.
notes: Page tested by another session (S1); recorded as a finding only. The page's own gap 1 already uses the narrower 'anaesthetic-only' wording, so the intent here is probably anaesthetic-only; as written, 'one wheal protocol with a local anaesthetic and a pain outcome' leaves out Cui 2017, a published randomised protocol of repeated intracutaneous injections containing the page's own drug. The section goes on to call intradermal botulinum toxin for painful diabetic neuropathy 'the nearest randomised design'; Cui 2017 is a randomised repeated intracutaneous design with the same anaesthetic (plus a steroid, in acute zoster), which the main session may weigh. No regimen detail is given here on purpose.

section: Sources > What has no source (last item)
sentence_as_it_stands: Any comparison of these drugs against the intradermal wheals he already uses. No trial has ever compared a systemic drug against a local-anaesthetic infiltration protocol in this or any neuropathy.
quote: Subjects were randomized to receive local methylcobalamin injection (N = 33), oral methylcobalamin (N = 33), or subcutaneous [dose figure omitted] lidocaine injection (N = 32) … oral methylcobalamin did not provide any significantly pain relief (P > 0.05).

One randomised trial has compared a systemic drug with a local-anaesthetic infiltration protocol in a neuropathic pain condition: oral methylcobalamin against repeated subcutaneous lidocaine injection, beside local methylcobalamin injection, in subacute herpetic neuralgia (Xu 2013, PMID 23566267).

page: 2 — Reference — Topical Treatments for Small Fiber Neuropathy
section: 3.2 · What the substitution cannot be measured against (the 'Ropivacaine' anchor bullet)
sentence_as_it_stands: Ropivacaine: the trial literature is perioperative prevention of chronic pain, not treatment of established pain, and is mixed — negative in 236 breast-surgery patients (P=0.37), weakly positive in 52 craniotomy patients.
quote: In the current study, we compared the effects of intracutaneous injections with ropivacaine and methylprednisolone in addition to standard treatment of antiviral and oral analgesics with standard treatment in 93 HZ patients for the prevention of PHN. … In the current study, intracutaneous injection using local anesthetics plus corticosteroids resulted in lower pain intensity (VAS) and fewer doses of rescue drug (tramadol) at each follow-up time point
corrected_wording: Ropivacaine: the trial literature by infiltration includes perioperative prevention of chronic pain (mixed — negative in 236 breast-surgery patients, weakly positive in 52 craniotomy patients), randomised trials of intracutaneous ropivacaine mixed with methylprednisolone in acute herpes zoster with pain and postherpetic-neuralgia outcomes (Cui 2017, PMID 27492741; Cui 2018, PMID 29153295), and repeated subcutaneous trigger-point injections added to carbamazepine in trigeminal neuralgia (Lemos 2010, PMID 21197324).
notes: Cui 2017 (this paper) and Cui 2018 are randomised trials of ropivacaine given into the skin, outside the perioperative setting, treating acute zoster pain and aiming to prevent PHN; the steroid is co-injected. Lemos 2010 is the main session's own source for refuting D070 (randomised, ropivacaine subcutaneously at trigger points in trigeminal neuralgia, an established chronic pain) and is named here from that record, not re-read. The same section's 'two further randomised trials exist in adjacent indications' also understates the skin-route trials in zoster and postherpetic neuralgia (Cui 2017 and 2018; Xiao 2010; Xu 2013; Amjad 2005; Ni 2017), most of them with a steroid or another active agent in the injection; recorded here rather than as a separate finding. The section's first sentence (no randomised trial in established small fibre neuropathy) stands. The same Reference page repeats D070's sentence in section 4.9 ('no study of cutaneous or subcutaneous ropivacaine infiltration exists in any chronic pain condition'), a second location of an error the main session's D070 refutation (Lemos 2010) already covers; Cui (acute zoster) adds nothing to that one.

page: 2 — Reference — Topical Treatments for Small Fiber Neuropathy
sentence_as_it_stands: No randomised trial of cutaneous or subcutaneous local anaesthetic infiltration for established chronic peripheral neuropathic pain was located for lidocaine, procaine or ropivacaine, so there is no published duration of analgesia per session against which a topical substitute could be measured, and no evidence on whether repeated infiltration is cumulative or diminishing.
quote: We investigated the therapeutic benefits of BTX-A in subjects with PHN in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Sixty subjects with PHN were randomly and evenly distributed into BTX-A, lidocaine, and placebo groups. After randomization, one of the following solutions was injected subcutaneously in the affected dermatome: [dose figure omitted] BTX-A, [dose figure omitted] lidocaine, or [dose figure omitted] saline (placebo).
corrected_wording: Randomised trials that include subcutaneous or locally infiltrated lidocaine in postherpetic neuralgia exist, with lidocaine as a comparator arm — against saline and botulinum toxin (Xiao 2010, PMID 21134121) and against a lidocaine–triamcinolone combination (Amjad 2005, PMID 16300701); none reports a duration of analgesia per session, so there is still no published per-session duration against which a topical substitute could be measured.
notes: Rests on an extra study (Xiao 2010) found by a PubMed search prompted by Cui 2017 (S-686-05), not from Cui's reference list; quote from its cached abstract. Amjad 2005 is in the main session's T02 record and the Health Pages - Meta receipt; named from there. The clause's consequence (no per-session duration of analgesia to compare against) stands. The last clause ('no evidence on whether repeated infiltration is cumulative or diminishing') sits uneasily beside section 4.9's 'Repeated infiltration is cumulative, not diminishing', but Amjad's falling lidocaine-only response was measured after the injection course ended, so it does not decide either; noted, not judged. Cui 2017 itself does not bear here: its population was acute zoster, not established chronic pain.

page: What is still unsettled across these pages, and what would settle each one
section: Which primary sources are unread, and what each would settle — Full text of J Anesth Clin Res 2012;3(3):199 (also summarised under 'The recommendation')
sentence_as_it_stands: The paper is paywalled and its eight primary references are the closest thing that exists to evidence for repeated intradermal wheals as a technique in use. [The recommendation: 'A second paywalled paper's reference list is the closest thing that exists to evidence for repeated intradermal wheals as a technique']
quote: Ninety-three patients with acute thoracic HZ were randomly assigned to receive a standard treatment of antiviral medication with p.o. analgesics or the standard treatment with the addition of repetitive intracutaneous injections of a local anesthetic and steroid mixture.
corrected_wording: The paper is paywalled and its eight primary references are unread. Published evidence on repeated intradermal injection as a technique also exists outside that reference list: a randomised trial of repeated intracutaneous local anaesthetic–steroid injections in acute herpes zoster (Cui 2017, PMID 27492741) and an uncontrolled series of repeated intradermal lidocaine wheal sessions in notalgia paresthetica (Mülkoğlu 2020, PMID 32416719).
notes: Cui 2017 is a randomised trial of repeated intracutaneous injection sessions with clinical outcomes, which is more direct evidence on repeated intradermal injection as a technique than an unread review reference list; by the Relief page's own account, the 2012 analysis reported outcomes after 'the single skin anesthesia treatment' and excluded zoster under three months. Mülkoğlu 2020 is already in the record elsewhere as the one anaesthetic-only wheal protocol with an outcome. Medium because the page orders its open questions by this ('The unread primary sources move first, because they bear on the technique in daily use'). The open question itself (what the eight papers are) is not answered by Cui. Cell-culture toxicity figures elsewhere on this page were not copied.

page: Results (neural therapy study summaries; child of 'Research')
section: A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Multifaceted Integrated Complementary-Alternative Therapy for Chronic Herpes Zoster-Related Pain
sentence_as_it_stands: Main Authors: Stefan Weinschenk, et al.
quote: The CAM therapies used were acupuncture, neural therapy ([dose figure omitted] procaine injection as a local anesthetic), cupping and bleeding, and TCM herbs. An immediate treatment group (n=32) received the CAM intervention [dose figure omitted]. A wait-list (delayed treatment) group (n=27) was used as a control
corrected_wording: Main authors: Fred Hui, Eleanor Boyle, Eugene Vayda, Richard H Glazier (Altern Med Rev 2012;17(1):57-68, PMID 22502623).
notes: Not a Cui 2017 finding: the page surfaced in the herpes-zoster searches run for this paper, and the trial it describes was checked on PubMed (it is already in claim A054's records under first author Hui). PubMed lists the authors as Hui F, Boyle E, Vayda E, Glazier RH; Weinschenk is not an author. The quote shows the design; the author list is from the PubMed record (not part of the abstract text the quote checker reads).

page: Results (neural therapy study summaries; child of 'Research')
section: A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Multifaceted Integrated Complementary-Alternative Therapy for Chronic Herpes Zoster-Related Pain
sentence_as_it_stands: 56 patients with a median pain duration of 4.8 months (some up to 15 years) were randomized. The immediate treatment group received [dose figure omitted] Procaine Neural Therapy [dose figure omitted]. ... Pain scores (VAS) dropped significantly from 7.2 to 2.3 within the first three weeks. ... This provides objective proof that repeated Procaine blockades can force a long-lasting "reset" of the sensory system in fiber-mediated neuropathic pain.
quote: The CAM therapies used were acupuncture, neural therapy ([dose figure omitted] procaine injection as a local anesthetic), cupping and bleeding, and TCM herbs. An immediate treatment group (n=32) received the CAM intervention [dose figure omitted]. A wait-list (delayed treatment) group (n=27) was used as a control
corrected_wording: A randomised, unblinded wait-list-controlled trial in 59 people with zoster-related pain of at least 30 days (32 treated immediately, 27 on a wait-list) tested a package of acupuncture, procaine neural therapy, cupping and bleeding, and Chinese herbs over three weeks. At three weeks pain was 2.3 in the treated group against 7.2 on the wait-list (baseline 7.5 and 7.8), and the reduction was maintained to two years. Because procaine was one part of a four-part package against no treatment, the trial cannot attribute the effect to procaine.
notes: Not a Cui 2017 finding: page surfaced in the herpes-zoster searches for this paper; checked against the PubMed abstract. The page describes the intervention as procaine neural therapy alone; the abstract names four therapies given together. 'From 7.2 to 2.3' pairs the wait-list group's three-week score with the treated group's (the treated group fell from 7.5). The abstract gives 59 randomised; 56 may be an analysed count from the full text, not checked. 'Objective proof that repeated Procaine blockades can force a long-lasting reset' goes further than an unblinded multi-therapy trial against a wait-list allows. The treatment frequency and procaine strength on the page are masked here.

section: 2. Xu et al. (2013/2015) - Local vs. Systemic Methylcobalamin for Herpetic Neuralgia
sentence_as_it_stands: This rigorous single-center randomized controlled trial assessed 98 patients (aged ≥ 50) with subacute herpetic neuralgia—a viral condition known to aggressively destroy A-delta and C-fibers. Patients were randomized to receive either local subcutaneous injections of methylcobalamin ([dose figure omitted]) plus lidocaine, intramuscular methylcobalamin, or oral methylcobalamin for [dose figure omitted]. ... The incidence of postherpetic neuralgia was 1.1% at 3 months.
quote: Subjects were randomized to receive local methylcobalamin injection (N = 33), oral methylcobalamin (N = 33), or subcutaneous [dose figure omitted] lidocaine injection (N = 32) … oral methylcobalamin did not provide any significantly pain relief (P > 0.05).
corrected_wording: Xu 2013 (PMID 23566267), a single-centre randomised trial in 98 people aged 50 or over with subacute herpetic neuralgia, compared local methylcobalamin injection, oral methylcobalamin and subcutaneous lidocaine injection; local methylcobalamin did best and oral methylcobalamin gave no significant relief. Local methylcobalamin combined with lidocaine against intramuscular methylcobalamin with local lidocaine, and a postherpetic-neuralgia incidence at 3 months, come from the same group's later trials in acute herpetic neuralgia (Xu 2015, PMID 26200815; Xu 2016, PMID 26814241).
notes: Rests on an extra study (Xu 2013) found by a PubMed search prompted by Cui 2017 (S-686-05); the page surfaced in a Notion search for that study's topic. The entry merges trials: its n, population, responder counts and 'oral routes did not provide any significant relief' match Xu 2013's abstract, but Xu 2013's third arm was subcutaneous lidocaine alone, not intramuscular methylcobalamin, and its arms did not combine methylcobalamin with lidocaine; the combination-versus-intramuscular design is Xu 2015 and Xu 2016, and '1.1% at 3 months' is in Xu 2016's abstract (Xu 2015's gives 2.04%). The author list likewise merges both groups' bylines. The lidocaine-only arm matters elsewhere in the record: it is what makes Xu 2013 a trial comparing a systemic drug with a local-anaesthetic infiltration protocol (claim A054). Methylcobalamin and treatment-length figures masked.
